summary: Describes mechanisms for transmitting IPv6 packets over Frame Relay networks. It was later updated by RFC 8064.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2590 says how to send IPv6 packets over Frame Relay. It gives the frame layout, a way to build an IPv6 address for each virtual circuit, and the two ways a neighbour discovery message can name the far end of a circuit.

subtitle: How to carry IPv6 on Frame Relay, with a separate address for each virtual circuit.

tldr.problem: Frame Relay is a network of virtual circuits, and IPv6 needs a defined way to travel over one. Nothing said how to frame IPv6 packets, how to form a link-local address, or how to name the far end of a circuit in a neighbour discovery message.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies the NLPID frame format, a 64-bit interface identifier built from a DLCI and a locally unique part, the link-local address built from it, and two formats for the link-layer address option that carries either a DLCI or a Frame Relay address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2590 is a Proposed Standard from May 1999 and has been updated by RFC 8064.

facts.label: Interface identifier layout
facts.value: 2 bits EUI, 38 bits Mid, 24 bits DLCI

today: RFC 2590 is a Proposed Standard from May 1999 and has been updated by RFC 8064. It remains the specification for carrying IPv6 over Frame Relay networks.

sections.title: What the RFC Specifies
sections.content:
The RFC specifies the frame format for transmission of IPv6 packets over Frame Relay networks, the method of forming IPv6 link-local addresses on Frame Relay links, and the mapping of IPv6 addresses to Frame Relay addresses. It also specifies the content of the Source/Target link-layer address option used in Neighbour Discovery and Inverse Neighbour Discovery messages sent over a Frame Relay link. It is part of a set of specifications that define these mechanisms for non-broadcast multiple access media and for specific link layers.

The information applies to Frame Relay devices that act as end stations, called DTEs, on a public or private Frame Relay network. End stations can be IPv6 hosts or routers, and the RFC calls them nodes.

Frame Relay networks hold a number of virtual circuits forming the connections between attached stations. The resulting set of interconnected devices forms a private Frame Relay group, which may be fully interconnected with a complete mesh of virtual circuits or only partially interconnected. Either way, each virtual circuit is uniquely identified at each Frame Relay interface by a Data Link Connection Identifier, or DLCI. In most circumstances a DLCI has strictly local significance at each interface. A virtual circuit behaves like a virtual link with its own parameters, separate from other circuits on the same wire: input and output maximum frame size, requested and agreed throughput, acceptable throughput, burst size and frame rate.

By default a DLCI is 10 bits long. The Frame Relay specifications also define 16, 17 and 23 bit DLCIs. The 16 bit form is not used, and the 17 and 23 bit forms are suggested for use with switched virtual circuits. The mechanisms in the RFC apply to both permanent and switched virtual circuits, whether they are point to point or point to multipoint.
sections.plainLanguage: A Frame Relay network connects devices with virtual circuits, and each circuit has a number, the DLCI, that only means something at the local interface. The RFC covers how IPv6 packets are framed, how each circuit gets its own IPv6 address, and how a neighbour discovery message names the far end of a circuit.

sections.title: Maximum Transmission Unit
sections.content:
The IPv6 minimum MTU is defined in the IPv6 specification. Frame Relay devices are generally configured with a maximum frame size of at least 1600 octets, so the default IPv6 MTU for a Frame Relay interface is 1592. A smaller frame size can be configured, but never below the IPv6 minimum MTU.

A larger size can be configured to avoid fragmentation. The maximum frame size is limited by the checksum mechanism at the HDLC level: CRC16 protects frames up to 4096 bytes, which reduces the effective maximum frame size to about 4088 bytes. A larger frame size, such as the one used by FDDI or Token Ring, would need CRC32, which is not yet widely used and is not mandatory for Frame Relay systems that follow the Frame Relay Forum and ITU-T standards.

If the upper layers provide enough error detection, an implementation may allow a frame size larger than 4080 octets with a weaker link-layer check. But because IPv6 relies on error detection at both the upper and lower layers, configuring the IPv6 MTU above 4080 is strongly discouraged.

Although a Frame Relay circuit allows separate maximum frame sizes for input and output, this specification assumes symmetry, with the same MTU in both directions. An implementation may also limit the maximum frame size to the interface level, in which case it applies to all the permanent and switched circuits on that interface. For a switched circuit, the maximum frame size negotiated during setup will not exceed the configured maximum.
sections.plainLanguage: The default IPv6 packet size on Frame Relay is 1592 octets, because the hardware is normally set up for frames of at least 1600. Larger frames are possible but the link checksum limits them, and the RFC discourages going above 4080.

sections.title: The IPv6 Frame Format
sections.content:
The encapsulation follows the multiprotocol interconnect specification for Frame Relay, which lets a virtual circuit carry IPv6 packets along with packets of other protocols. The NLPID frame format is used, in which the IPv6 NLPID has the value 0x8E. The frame carries a Q.922 address of length n, which is either 2 or 4 octets, then a Control field with the value 0x03, then the NLPID 0x8E, then the IPv6 packet, then the frame check sequence.

The Q.922 representation of a DLCI, in canonical order, places the first bit in the least significant, that is the right-most, bit of a byte in memory. The RFC shows the three layouts. For a 10 bit DLCI, the first octet holds the high-order part of the DLCI with two zero bits, and the second octet holds the low-order part with four bits set to 0001. The 17 bit and 23 bit layouts extend the same pattern over more octets, with the final octet of the 23 bit form carrying the last part of the DLCI and the bit pattern 01.

The encapsulation of data and control messages that use SNAP encapsulation with their own protocol identifiers is not affected. The encoding of the IPv6 protocol identifier in such messages must be done according to the specifications of those protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Each frame carries a Q.922 address, a control byte, the byte 0x8E that says IPv6 follows, then the IPv6 packet. The DLCI inside the Q.922 address is written in a fixed bit order.

sections.title: The Pseudo-Interface Identifier
sections.content:
An interface identifier for an IPv6 Frame Relay interface must be unique on a Frame Relay link and on each of the virtual links formed by the circuits terminated on that interface. The identifier is locally generated by the IPv6 module.

Because each virtual circuit is configured or established separately and acts like an independent virtual link, the RFC treats the termination point of each circuit on the interface as a pseudo-interface or logical-interface. That makes it useful to give each DLCI its own autoconfigured address, including its own link-local address.

The interface identifier is built from three fields. The EUI bits are bits 6 and 7 of the first octet, standing for the EUI-64 universal/local and individual/group bits converted for IPv6 use. The universal/local bit is set to zero, because the 64-bit interface identifier has only local significance, and the individual/group bit is set to zero to reflect a unicast address. The Mid field is 38 bits wide and exists to add uniqueness. The DLCI field is 24 bits and may hold a 10, 17 or 23 bit DLCI value, which must be extended with zeros to 24 bits. A DLCI-based identifier should be generated as a result of successfully establishing a circuit. If the DLCI is not known, the field must be set to the unspecified DLCI value, which sets each of the 24 bits to one.

Because DLCIs are local to a Frame Relay node, two distinct virtual circuits elsewhere in the network can have the same DLCI value.

The RFC suggests two ways to generate the Mid field. The first merges a random 6-bit number, a 16-bit Frame Relay Node Identifier that the user administers to identify a node locally, and a 16-bit Frame Relay Link Identifier that numerically represents the interface or link. The second takes the Frame Relay address: if the interface has an E.164 or X.121 number, or an NSAP address, the Mid must be the number formed from it, encoded in binary coded decimal or binary and truncated to 38 bits. Since the interface identifier has only local significance, the truncation can be on the high-order or the low-order bits, and the RFC suggests trying the high-order bits first and the low-order bits if that does not give uniqueness on the link.

Duplicate Address Detection from the IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration specification is used repeatedly during the generation process, until the identifier, and with it the link-local address on the link, is unique.
sections.plainLanguage: Each virtual circuit on an interface is treated as a separate pseudo-interface and gets its own 64-bit identifier. The identifier holds two bits of flags, a 38-bit part that makes it unique on the link, and the 24-bit DLCI of the circuit.

sections.title: Link-Local Addresses
sections.content: The IPv6 link-local address for a Frame Relay interface is formed by appending the interface identifier described above to the prefix FE80::/64. The prefix is ten bits of 1111111010, then 54 zero bits, then the 64-bit Frame Relay interface identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The link-local address is the fixed prefix FE80::/64 followed by the 64-bit identifier of the circuit.

sections.title: Address Mapping for Neighbour Discovery
sections.content:
The procedure for mapping IPv6 addresses to link-layer addresses is described in the IPv6 neighbour discovery specification, and the extensions that map link-layer addresses back to IPv6 addresses are called Inverse Neighbour Discovery. This RFC defines the formats of the link-layer address fields used in those messages. It does not define an algorithmic mapping of IPv6 multicast addresses to Frame Relay link-layer addresses.

An IPv6 address can map to two kinds of identifier that are equivalent to link-layer addresses: DLCIs and Frame Relay addresses. So the RFC defines two distinct formats for the link-layer address field.

The DLCI Format is used in messages on circuits that were established before the exchange, mostly permanent virtual circuits. On switched circuits it makes sense with Inverse Neighbour Discovery, used after a switched circuit is established to learn the other IPv6 addresses assigned to the remote node. Its value field has two parts. The address type is encoded in the first two bits of the first two octets, and both bits are set to one to indicate the DLCI format; the remaining bits in those two octets are not used and must be zero on transmit and ignored on receipt. The DLCI itself is encoded as a Q.922 address, padded with zeros to the last octet of the six octets available for the whole link-layer address field. The option type is 1 for a source link-layer address and 2 for a target link-layer address, and the length is 1 in units of 8 octets.

The Frame Relay Address Format is used mostly before a new switched circuit is established, to get the mapping from the remote node's Frame Relay identifier to a certain IPv6 address. Its value field has three parts, and the RFC lists four. The address type is encoded in the first two bits of the first octet, with the first bit set to zero and the second set to one. The size is encoded in the last, high-order, six bits of the first octet. The Address Family Number identifies the family of the address. The address itself is an E.164 or X.121 number in binary coded decimal, two digits per octet, or an NSAP address. With an odd number of digits, the lowest order digit fills only half of an octet and the rest of the field is padded with zeros. The option length may be 2 for numbers or NSAP addresses of at most 11 octets, 3 for NSAP addresses longer than 11 but no longer than 19 octets, and 4 for NSAP addresses longer than 19 octets.

An implementation may hold both kinds of identifier in its neighbour discovery cache, and where two nodes share several circuits, one node's cache may map the remote node's IPv6 address to each DLCI in turn. The RFC leaves the mechanisms that make those distinctions out of scope. The override bit in advertisement messages should behave as the neighbour discovery specification requires, and an implementation should override one address format in its cache with the same type of address format.
sections.plainLanguage: A neighbour discovery message can name the far end of a circuit in two ways: by the DLCI of the circuit, or by the Frame Relay address of the node. The RFC gives the bit layout of both options.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Neighbour Discovery Messages
sections.content:
Frame Relay networks do not provide link-layer multicasting, so multicast has to be emulated for neighbour discovery to work. A node must send frames carrying neighbour discovery multicast packets to all the virtual circuits on a Frame Relay interface. That applies to messages addressed both to the all-node and to the solicited-node multicast addresses. The method works well with permanent virtual circuits. A mesh of permanent circuits may be configured and dedicated to multicast traffic only, and a set of point-to-multipoint permanent circuits is an alternative to a mesh.

On the receiving side, the DLCI fields in a neighbour discovery message have local significance, and the DLCI at the sender is not the DLCI at the receiver. The sender may not even know the receiver's DLCI. So when a node receives a Neighbour Solicitation carrying a source link-layer address option with a DLCI, the message must undergo Frame Relay specific preprocessing before the neighbour discovery engine handles it. The preprocessing stores, in the source link-layer address option, the DLCI of the virtual circuit on which the frame arrived, as the receiver knows it, encoded in the appropriate format. How that value is passed from the Frame Relay module to the preprocessing module is an implementation choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Frame Relay has no native group delivery, so a node sends neighbour discovery multicast messages on every one of its circuits. On receipt, the node replaces the DLCI in the message with the one that identifies the circuit it arrived on, because the numbers differ on each side.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The mechanisms for generating an IPv6 Frame Relay interface identifier are intended to give uniqueness at the level of the virtual circuit. Protection against duplication comes from the IPv6 stateless autoconfiguration Duplicate Address Detection mechanisms. Protection against forgery or accident at the level of these mechanisms comes from the IPv6 security mechanisms applied to neighbour discovery and inverse neighbour discovery messages.

The RFC adds an ordering requirement. To avoid an authentication verification failure, the Frame Relay specific preprocessing of a Neighbour Solicitation that carries a DLCI format source link-layer address option must be done by the receiver after it has completed IP security processing.
sections.plainLanguage: The identifier scheme only makes addresses unique; it does not protect them. Forgery is handled by the IP security mechanisms, and the receiver must check the message before it rewrites the DLCI inside it.
